utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Draca, as well. I'd like to remind you, as you may have noticed I always do in the morning, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. I even yesterday had to remind you of what the whole truth was. Please keep that in mind. Mr. Farr, if you're ready, the two hours you need will start now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Draca.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I still have a number of topics to get through so I would ask you to keep your answers as brief as possible while still providing a fair answer. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to your evidence about Skabrnja and particularly to the forces involved in the attack on Skabrnja. At transcript page 16746, you described the forces you believed to have participated in that attack. And you said: "It was the 180th Motorised Brigade from Benkovac, reinforced with one company of the TO Benkovac and was subordinated to the brigade command which was under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we now please have Exhibit P2082 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this is an operative information from the Benkovac Department of the SAO Krajina MUP SDB. It's dated 11 November, 1991, when you were the head of the Benkovac SDB. It discusses events that occurred on the 8th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And if we could have the bottom of the page in English, and the middle of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I'm interested in a portion that begins with the word: "At about 1500 hours of the same day." That portion reads: "At about 1500 hours of the same day, to Benkovac TO Staff, there arrived Colonel Kasum and Lieutenant-Colonel Vuletic with the retinue TO Krajina staff members. Talking to the Benkovac STO, or TO staff commander, Colonel Kasum made a very interesting remark. He claimed that the special units which were in the phase of being created, including the Benkovac SUP anti-terrorist unit, must carry out a special assignment in a few days, and after that, the police organs would again be under the commands of Krajina TO Staffs." Sir, my question to you is just the following. The Benkovac SUP was in the process of forming a special unit at this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With a brief explanation. These people were engage in regular police work, but those who were younger among them would be assigned to the specialist anti-terrorist platoon. But it was a small platoon, some 30 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we now please have Exhibit P1212 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, before you is the duty roster from the Benkovac police station. The date of this document is 18 October 1991. That date appears on the last page of the document. The heading of the document indicates that the duty roster is based on a new organisation introduced in the Benkovac SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have the bottom of page 8 of the B/C/S and the middle of page 9 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, before us we have a list of 14 names with the heading: "Special Unit." This is the special unit that you were just telling us about; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And the first name on the list is Goran Opacic. He was the head of this special unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a while. But sometime in autumn of that year, he transferred to the army. But I don't know which date exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have the next page in both languages and the top half of each page initially.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, under the heading: "Military Police," I'm interested in the name Milan Burza. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an inspector at the Benkovac SUP even before the war. And sometime in 1993, I think, he moved to state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we now have the bottom half of that page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Under the heading: "In TO Units," in the second section, one of the names we see is Bosko Drazic, the SJB chief. Is it correct that this list indicates that Bosko Drazic had a role serving in or coordinating with TO units?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. As indicated in the previous document, the Krajina police was, in terms of hierarchy, within the command of the TO command, where it came to military conflicts. Each chief of station was, ex officio, a coordinator for the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we now have Exhibit P1209, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this is an Official Note from Lieutenant Commander Simo Rosic and Major Ostojic, dated the 8th of March, 1992. And it's related to events in Skabrnja and Nadin. I'm going to read a short portion of it, beginning at the beginning. "Having conducted several IR, or interviews, talks with personal and official contacts, and examined the unit's combat documentation, we have found out the following about the killing of civilians in Skabrnja and Nadin villages on 18 and 19 November 1991: "All the collected data shows that the killings were committed by the members of the Benkovac STO, that is Territorial Defence Staff, special units, or units that fought under their command. These were volunteers from Serbia and Opacic's group composed of combatants from this area." Sir, we've seen an Official Note from the Benkovac DB saying that the -- that the Benkovac special unit was going to have to undertake special tasks under the command of the TO. We've seen a list of the members of the special unit with Goran Opacic at its head, and now we've seen this JNA report stating that the data collected shows that Opacic's group, fighting under the Benkovac TO command, committed killings. The truth is that the Benkovac SUP special unit participated in the attack on Skabrnja and participated in the killing of civilians there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first document is dated the 11th of November. That's to say, seven days before the attack on Skabrnja. At that time, none of us knew that an attack was impending on Skabrnja. So I don't know the colonels who came from Knin, which tasks they were referring to. Knowing the situation at the time, I doubt seriously that a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel could order Opacic to do something of the sort seven days ahead of the attack. As far as Opacic's group is concerned, this Official Note was written on the 8th of March, that's to say, three or four months after Skabrnja. Simo Rosic, a naval captain, wrote it, who came from Pula to help Major Ristic, a man who was not very familiar with our areas. According to what I know about it, Goran Opacic was not involved in the attack on Skabrnja. Every soldier in our area knew it. Now, did he appear in the area afterwards when it was captured? That I don't know. I can tell you, however, for sure, that Opacic was not there on the day that the 180th Motorised Brigade conducted the attack, together with the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, Bosko Drazic also personally participated in the attack on Skabrnja that day; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. As you said, the police was within the Territorial Defence. If they had been engaged by the Territorial Defence, then the police did take part. I know that there was a TO company. I don't know what -- who it was comprised of. As far as Bosko Drazic is concerned, it is possible that he assigned some of his men to the TO, but I really doubt that as the head of the police station he would have participated in the attack and that the army would have allowed him to.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So just to make sure I understand you. You allow for the possibility that members of the police in Benkovac participated in the attack on Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, is it also correct that Goran Opacic had been trained at the Golubic camp?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, just so you're clear, our position is that Goran Opacic and Bosko Drazic both personally participated in the attack on that day. They're your close colleagues and it's because they're your close colleagues that you are unwilling to admit that they participated in the attack and in these crimes. If you'd like to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. We weren't close colleagues. I wanted Drazic's removal because I didn't think he was doing his job properly when it came to maintaining law and order. As for Opacic, at the time the conflicts were starting out, we weren't on good terms. So I cannot claim for Drazic whether he was there or not because I don't know for sure. But I do know, for sure, that -- that Drazic -- or, rather, that Opacic wasn't there, and I can even explain why I know that he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we'd like to hear the explanation of the witness. Please explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A day before the attack, I came across him in the town of Benkovac. He told me himself that he would not take part in the attack because he said that he had heard of a ploy by which military security wanted to stab him in the back. I asked him who his informant was because that would be a likely indicator of the reliability of the information. He refused to disclose the name. I went the following day to the barracks in the Benkovac Command, as the attack progressed, to see what exactly was going on, and I saw him outside the Benkovac barracks. So I'm talking about the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, whoever was involved in the attack on Skabrnja, we agree about the fact that there was a horrible massacre there, that the civilians were killed and that the village was more or less obliterated; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have 65 ter 5596.3 on the screen. The bottom of page 1 in both languages. And if we could scroll to the -- yeah. Thanks. The bottom of both page, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this is an entry from one of Mladic's notebooks. You were shown this portion on Tuesday, although you were shown a typed version of the Serbian rather than the handwritten original. Specifically, you were shown the portion of this entry where Mladic wrote: "180th Brigade to move to the okb, armoured battalion, a little towards Skabrnja and Nadin - to erase that." You were asked about what Colonel Mladic said at the meeting you attended, and you said: "My understanding was that the intention was to frighten them a bit." Now, we've just discussed the fact that what happened wasn't a little bit of frightening but the destruction of a village and a massacre. In other words, the so-called task written in Mr. Mladic's notebook matches the task, to use his word, that was actually carried out. Sir, the truth is, the plan was always to obliterate Skabrnja, and you knew that before the attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. We weren't able to know that. We weren't part of the military authority. Those who were acquainted with the situation in 1991, to a small extent, knew that the JNA did not disclose information or share it with the local civilian authorities. As for the attack itself, was it planned ahead and was it planned so as to produce such a large extent of destruction is something that I am not able to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you allow for the -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last sentence that the witness said was not interpreted. Can it be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll ask him to repeat. You said, Mr. Draca, that: "... for the attack itself, was it planned ahead and was it planned so as to produce such a large extent of destruction is something that I'm not able to know." Did you add anything then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I added, nor did the Yugoslav People's Army ever share any such information with those who were outside of its ranks, including the police and civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, just so we're clear, you do allow for the possibility that there was, in fact, a plan in advance to completely destroy the village. You just say that you have no knowledge, one way or the other; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, yes. I wasn't able to know the intentions and plans of an organisation that I didn't work for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this excerpt as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 5596 will receive number P3078, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Draca, could I ask you one question. The word "to erase" and "to frighten," do we agree that these are totally different terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree fully. But the term that is written here in the diary was not the one that he used at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say what he wrote was not what he said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just so the record is clear, the portion I just entered was 5596.3, rather than 5596.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, does that cause you any problems or is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. I will repeat. So document 5596.3 will receive number P3078, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is the document that was admitted under this number. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, during your direct examination you also discussed the murders of the civilians in Bruska in December of 1991 and the subsequent investigation. I'd like to show you an entry from another -- actually, I believe it's from the same notebook but a different portion a few days after the murders and ask you a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have P2934 on the screen. And, if possible, I'd like the top of page 3 of the original with the ERN J000-3755, and the top of page 3 of the English translation with the ERN J000-3582-ET. If we could please have page 3 of the English and of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, for your information, this portion, this entry is dated 24 December 1991. And I'd like you to take a look at the portion next to the entry for 1300 hours. It appears to say that it's recording something about someone named Kero. And just for clarity, the words -- or the letters KS and then the word "Zadar" appear next to his name. Does that indicate that Kero came from the Zadar Crisis Staff and, thus, was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing that last name for the first time, but it's possible. I'm not quite sure what that indicates.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: The entry says that Kero: "... requests that 11 dead bodies of Bruska village inhabitants be delivered to him, that they be enabled to evacuate approximately 2.000 inhabitants - Croats from Bruska, Rodaljice and other villages, under the supervision of the European Community Mission." Sir, the murder of 11 or so civilians in Bruska, including, as you said, a Serb who was your relative, caused a great deal of fear among the remaining Croatian civilians and caused a much greater number of Croat civilians to wish to leave the area; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, in fact, this happened every time that crimes were committed against civilians in the SAO Krajina. Every murder or other crime against a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, instead of general questions like this, I would ask for a specific question to be put, which departure by citizens, which killings. We would like specific things rather than general things which do not make it possible for the witness to give a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may object to a question. If the question is so general that the witness is unable to answer it because of this character of the question, then the witness will tell us that he's -- that he's unable to answer such a broad question. He has not done so yet. At the same time, Mr. Farr, it might save you time as well, to come to specifics as soon as possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, during your direct examination, you testified about a number of crimes committed against non-Serb civilians in the SAO Krajina. With respect to Bruska, you've just confirmed that those crimes caused a much larger number of Croat civilians to wish to flee. With respect to all crimes against non-Serb civilians that you have knowledge of, is it correct that the majority of those crimes caused a much larger number of Croat civilians to wish to flee?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you put that just now can apply to all the peoples in all of the wars. Unfortunately, you are correct. When I say "unfortunately," what I mean is that there were a large number of civilian casualties on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you'll be able to comment on this or not, but is it the case that the purpose of the people who committed these crimes was, in part, exactly that. In other words, these crimes were committed with the goal of causing the Croat civilian population to feel so insecure that they had no choice but to leave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I would echo Mr. Petrovic's objection earlier. I mean, if the witness says yes, does that mean he was aware that one person's objective was to do that. Or if he says yes, is he saying, "I was aware that everybody's objective" -- I mean the answer is -- the question is general. The answer is inevitably general and unhelpful, we would submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please split up. It's a whole line of reasoning for which you asked the witness's confirmation, and even if he says, yes, or if he says no -- especially when he says yes, we would not be certain that he has included all the elements in your question so rather take them one by one. I see you're looking at the clock. Mr. Farr, that doesn't justify to produce evidence which causes more problems than it resolves. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour, and it's my fault. That's something that I should have put to the witness rather than -- rather than asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, it's our position that that's what happened. The people who committed these crimes did so in part with the intention that it cause Croat civilians to flee the SAO Krajina. If you have a comment. If not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is whether you agree with the statement of Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if the Trial Chamber is aware, but, in the meantime, the Croatian justice system processed the perpetrator, because a number of victims survived, and they know who the killer is. This is a very rough intelligent person from a remote area. I simply cannot believe that this man had such grandiose ideas regarding the commission of this crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, the fact that a crime is investigated is not necessarily an answer to what Mr. Farr put to you. Is that the people, not just one single person, that committed these crimes did it for the purposes as Mr. Farr told you. Do you agree with that, or do you say "I don't know," or what -- what's your position in relation to that proposal by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally think that that was not their motive, but, actually, I don't know. But, on the basis of what I can estimate, I don't think that that was their motive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Political motive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, you stand by that despite the fact that, according to you, the purpose of the attack on Skabrnja was to scare people a little; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood you correctly. If you're talking about the topic that we had at the meeting, I understood the intimidation to be -- to move the forward guards that were on the road. This is how I understood that term of frightening them off or intimidating them. But the attack was broader. As he says in the diary, "shake them up a bit," "razmrdati" [phoen]. It's a different term, to scare them a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, discussing the events -- or, rather, the investigation in Bruska, at transcript page 16765, you stated: "Yes, from the very start, there was a thorough investigation conducted, and a dozen suspects were investigated. I was in contact with public security and I was therefore privy to the course of the investigation." Were any of those dozen suspects members of the Krajina police?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one was a member of the reserves for a few months, but when the crime was actually committed, that person had not been coming to work already for over a month, so he was no longer considered a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: In discussing the events in Bruska you said: "There were no eye-witnesses. The villagers of Bruska who may have had some information left for Zadar in the meantime and no statements were taken from them." That's at transcript page 16765. You also mention oral information received from one of the victims, a survivor, who was in the hospital. Is it your position that no written statement was ever taken from a survivor of the Bruska massacre?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if the survivor gave a written statement to the military security organs. I'm not aware whether he did or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, I feel an obligation to inform you that I misspoke at the beginning of this session. You know that the last words yesterday was: "One hour, Mr. Farr," and then you said, "yes." So when I said two hours this morning, that was not exactly what I had on my mind, and I see it from your smile that you were aware that it was one hour instead of two.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: I didn't dare to hope, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you've just said you don't know if the survivor gave a written statement to the military security organs. Do you know whether any survivor ever gave a written statement to the Benkovac Public Security Station, the station where you worked?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were at the hospital in Knin later, and they were guarded. The Benkovac SUP, I don't know if they took any statements. As far as I know, I don't think that they did, but I really couldn't say definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit P43 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this is an official record of the Knin SUP public security service, Benkovac. As you can see, it's dated the 25th of December, 1991, four days after the events in Bruska.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to the bottom, please. Next page in English. Apologies. Bottom in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, as you can see, this record was taken by Milan Burza, a man who earlier today you identified as an inspector of the Benkovac SJB. You also indicated that he was a member of state security from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: If we could go back to the first page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And I'm interested in the portion beginning with the words: "It may have been around 2000 hours when we heart a knock at the front door ..." I'll read that portion now. "It may have been around 2000 hours when we heard a knock at the front door of our house. I got up from the table, went to the [sic] door and asked who it was. An unfamiliar male voice responded: The police, the police. Since I did not recognise the voice, I told Dragan to go and see who that was. Dragan asked who it was, and the same unfamiliar voice responded: The Krajina police. We heard a burst of gun-fire in front of our door. And then our mother said we should flee." Sir, it's true that this statement does not mention perpetrators by name but this was certainly a sufficient basis to begin an investigation as to whether the perpetrators were members of the Krajina police; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Didn't I say that there was an investigation carried out? That included all the potential perpetrators from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you did say that. But a moment ago when I asked you whether any of those individuals were members of the Krajina police, I believe that you just said that there was one who was a reserve member who hadn't been at his post. Was there any further follow-up on this statement?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just said at the beginning, all the potential perpetrators. And when we narrowed it down to these people, then we understood that one of them was a former member of the reserve forces of the police. When I say "former," what I mean is that by not coming to work for more than a month, he willingly was no longer a member of the police. So I have to say that during period everybody wore uniforms. Everybody said that they were this or that. There were people who were in the police for seven days and then did not appear for a year and then continued to wear the uniform regardless of that. It wasn't really a state with the rule of law that you would see in regular circumstances. I also have to add that, had this not been organised by the police of the Serbian Krajina, then their inspector would not have written a report like this. Based on this, you can see the sincere desire of the police to get to the bottom of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Was it based on this report that you identified the reserve member of the Krajina police as a potential suspect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would kindly ask the question to be interpreted to the witness again because the B/C/S interpretation was not quite correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least you have an impression that there may have been a mistake in the translation. Let's slowly repeat the question. The question was, Mr. Draca, whether you identified the reserve member of the Krajina police as a potential suspect on the basis of this report, which is now on your screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not on the basis of this report. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may I take it that the question is on what basis then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of oral statements of survivors taken individually. People were frightened. They were scared to give statements, and we understood that. And you simply could not force somebody to sign a statement that could potentially prompt some kind of retaliation, and they couldn't say something that they were not sure of. Simply, people had confidence in us and they said who they had seen close to the village on that day, that morning, that evening. They didn't have specific facts as indicating that somebody had been caught in the middle of firing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat. You said: "They didn't have specifically facts as indicating that somebody had been caught in the middle of firing ..." What did you then add? Because the interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the facts were known exclusively to the survivors. But they were already in hospital in Knin, so they could not tell that to the rest of the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you then seriously investigate what may have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a great desire to assist this investigation but the public security service was conducting the investigation, especially the inspectors from Knin because it was a major incident. So I don't know all the details as to whether statements were taken and in what form from people who were victims, who were wounded and were at the Knin hospital. I assume that it's possible that such statements were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the first and very important step in such an investigation would be to collect the cartridges and the bullets found at the place where people had told you that shots were fired.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a serious on-scene investigation was taken, by taking photographs, taking all sort of prints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about cartridges and bullets. Were they collected, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A large number of casings were found, and you could see that the fire came from different kinds of weapons. After that, there were interviews, and some facilities owned by persons who were suspected were even interviewed [as interpreted]. But, however, there was no forensics institute in the Krajina, so I think that this was never sent to the institute in Belgrade. I don't know why. And it was a question whether they would have accepted that at the time. So we had no opportunity to thoroughly investigate the finger-prints and the ballistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could have secured the weapons of at least that one suspect or other suspects; especially also weapons of the special police unit members, isn't it? And, then, do the investigation at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the places where searches were conducted and interviews taken, the weapons were confiscated, as you said, and placed in the security station in Knin. I add probably, because I was not responsible for the investigation and did not directly participate in it. We just were involved on our own from time to time, so that I was not fully updated about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, just to be clear, do you maintain your position that you were never aware of this statement, despite the fact that Milan Burza was an inspector in the Benkovac SJB and despite the fact that he worked for state security, starting in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was taken two years before he came to Benkovac. Perhaps at that point in time I did know, but it's 20 years since then so I cannot recall seeing it before, this statement. But I do know that steps were taken. Actions were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: And, sir, just to clarify your last answer. You said it was taken two years before he came to Benkovac. What you meant was two years before he joined the state security in Benkovac, he had previously been an inspector in the Benkovac police station; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I made a slip. Two years before he transferred to the DB. He was a permanent resident of Benkovac. He lived there permanently.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 4293 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, this is a dispatch from Milan Martic to the SFRY Presidency, the federal SUP, the Supreme Defence Council, Croatian MUP, and the Serbian Republican SUP. And I'm just going to read the first paragraph. It says: "Based on verified information received by Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina state security, that on 15 February 1991, the concentrated special unit of MUP RH, with around 150 members in possession of vehicles and armaments was thrown into Plitvicka Jezera, so Titova Korenica. They represent the paramilitary formations in this region." Sir, as I understand it, you didn't join the SAO Krajina DB for a couple of months after this. But is it correct that this is one of the kinds of information that the SAO Krajina DB gathered when you were a member? Information about special units of the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Skipping the next two paragraphs, I'll read beginning with the words: "The possibility ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr, I'm a bit puzzled by the language used in this document. What you read was "thrown into Plitvicka Jezera." But it reads: "... was --"

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "-- thrown in in Plitvicka Jezera ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Which makes more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- there's some difficulty in understanding the double "in," but you didn't quote it accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And perhaps we'll get the translation confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, on that point, just very briefly, this document essentially says that the Croatian special unit, the special unit of the Croatian MUP, was put in the area of the Plitvice lakes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: So now beginning with the paragraph that starts with the words: "The possibility ..." "The possibility of armed conflict with unpredictable consequences is rather high unless the policemen withdraw from the territory of SAO Krajina. Thus, and compatible with your constitutional authorisations, we kindly ask and warn MUP RH Minister Boljkovac to take appropriate steps to prevent the unwelcome consequences. "If you do not follow the above written, we cannot be held responsible for the consequences." Sir, during your direct examination you gave a significant amount of evidence regarding potential threats posed to the Serbs in Croatia by the Croatian authorities. And to be clear, the Prosecution does not contest much of that evidence. But this document shows the other side of that story. This is a threat from Martic and the SAO Krajina authorities to the authorities of the Republic of Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group was infiltrated into an area where 100 per cent of the population were Serbs. You see that it was addressed to the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, and the request is asking them to retreat from the area because it would be a threat to everyone, including the Croats. The only thing is that at the bottom he says that he cannot assume responsibility for any consequences. By the way, let me tell you that during World War II, the entire male population was killed in that area, so to infiltrate people wearing an insignia from 1941 must mean that you would know that something like that would heighten tensions in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that Martic was determined that no armed force loyal to the Croatian government would remain anywhere in the SAO Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 4293 will receive number P3079, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P3079 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, before I finish my examination, I'm going to tell you the Prosecution position regarding you and your evidence so can you comment on it, if you choose. Our position is that you worked closely with and co-operated with Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic over a period of months or years. You supported the same goals as they did. They supported your activities and you supported theirs. Because of this, and because of gratitude for your job in the DB of Serbia, you wish to assist them as much as possible. While some aspects of your testimony have been truthful, you have been less than honest with the Court regarding certain matters that you think may implicate Mr. Simatovic or Mr. Stanisic. In particular, you have crafted your testimony to attempt to offer innocent explanations for otherwise incriminating facts. Would you like to comment or respond on that?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. I do not deny for a second that as two services, we did have very close co-operation at times, and at times there was no co-operation whatsoever. But let me note that all the institutions in the Republic of the Serbian Krajina had a similar sort of co-operation with all their equivalents in Serbia. You have to understand that we are one and the same people and they were our only ally in the war. Had we gone on to join some -- or, rather, had we gone on to unite with them along the lines of what we were discussing yesterday, well, I suppose there would be something to document that. As for my admittance into the Serbian DB, well, let me tell you that it wasn't all bed and roses. I should have perhaps sought employment elsewhere because I would have had a better pension. Now, as for Mr. Stanisic [as interpreted], I didn't see him all the way to Operation Pauk. All my dealings with Mr. Stanisic cannot be described as close co-operation. Not even in professional terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness first explained when he saw Mr. Simatovic and when -- and then the period during which he didn't see him. That's page 25, line 24. And then he moved on to speak of his contacts with Mr. Stanisic. So before the witness proceeds with his answer, perhaps we should have that corrected now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, did you include in your answer when you saw Mr. Simatovic and during which period you didn't see him? If that's the case, please tell us because it has not been translated to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since his departure in 1991, all the way through to his arrival during Operation Pauk, that was the three-year period. And then, if I can just make one more point. I am under the impression that somehow there is the wish to -- for me -- to induce me to say artificially that they were one and the same service and there is no documentation, there are no archives that could show that they weren't two services. I did say that, unfortunately, I would have wished them to be one and the same service, but that was not the case. And this was the case primarily for political reasons. We were professionals serving those higher up and we didn't have the powers to either unite or separate services.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: One further question, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Sir, you just said that, as I understood you, you understood -- you said that it was unfortunate that the two services were not one and the same and that you would have wished that. Why would you have wished that?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that would mean that the international community accepted the reality of us not being able to live in the Republic of Croatia. That would mean that the international community would allow our unification with Republika Srpska or the Republic of Serbia because it -- everybody was well aware of the fact that as small as we were, we weren't able to survive in the area on our own. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Mr. Draca, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a suggestion to take the break now, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: There is a suggestion, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will take the break now, and we will resume at 20 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for the late start. Mr. Jordash, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- further examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just a few more questions just to seek some clarification, if I can, Mr. Draca. First of all, picking up from where Mr. Farr left off, and your purported gratitude to Mr. Stanisic for the job he gave you. What job did you take in the Serbian DB precisely?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got the job of advisor in the Novi Sad centre. There were no posts available in the Belgrade centre at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Advisor to who?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Advisor to the chief of the state security centre in Novi Sad, which is roughly 100 kilometres away from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: With no operational contact with Stanisic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you've not been contacted by Mr. Stanisic to give evidence on his behalf, neither has anybody from his Defence team contacted you over the last five years; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Neither have you spoken to Mr. Stanisic over the last -- well, since his arrest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Earlier on, I said that I had not seen him since 1995, and the first time I saw him next was coming into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that's the first time -- no. Let me start that again. So am I correct that you hadn't spoken to him since 1995?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you didn't speak to him either between 1991 and 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was exactly that Mr. Stanisic came to visit the Plitvice Lakes National Park. I think it was 1994. So I didn't speak to him before 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was this, given your desire to unify the services, a source of frustration for you? You have this position in the RSK DB. You're not communicating, it seems, with the chief of the Serbian DB. What was your opinion about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was realistic. And I knew that it was politically unfeasible. So I wasn't particularly frustrated by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why was it politically unfeasible, in your view?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Prosecutor said, back in 1991, when Martic or the Serbian National Council and the Krajina government sought unification with Serbia, the parliament of the Republic of Serbia rejected the initiative, and not once was the possibility of unification with the Republic of Serbia mentioned again. I knew that it was impossible through contacts with many representatives of international missions in Knin because I saw that the world did not support it. So I knew that it was unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you've been quite clear that, if the Prosecution were to investigate the archives, they would not find any document to support their conclusion that there was a unification of the RSK DB and the Serbian DB. And we'll leave that to them. But what kind of documentation might there be if what the Prosecution said was true was, in fact, true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's not really an objection to the question per se. But it's a mischaracterisation of the Prosecution case. What we said was that they were functioning almost as a single service and that plans and preparations had been made to unify the services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it -- I think that's a second characterisation by the Prosecution. I mean, we had two days ago for the first time a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we have -- if it's on transcript, then if there is any dispute about how it was said, then we should rely on what we find in the transcript. If you have the source, then please use it, or take your time to find it. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take Mr. Farr's comment and I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- work with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Plans and preparations had been made to unify the services, according to the Prosecution. Would you agree with me that if there had been plans and preparations to unify the services, there would have been such things as discussions and documents indicating the organ -- proposed organisation for the unification? Documents dealing with the number of people that the new organisation was supposed to engage? The type and number of posts that the new organisation was supposed to engage? Things like that. Would you agree with me that those things would be the type of plans and preparations that would be necessary in light of an intention to unify two state services?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Had such plans been made, that would have made up for voluminous documentation. But I assert that there were no such documents, there is not a single witness who would say that there were initiatives to unify the services, let alone anything more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we'll leave that there and leave that to the Prosecution. Let me pick up on some issues concerning Martic and Kojic and Kostic. On the 2nd of February, at page 16890 of the transcript, you noted that Martic had discussed his idea that there were DB operatives in the Krajina and that you all thought it unacceptable that they should be present in your area without you knowing about it. Why was that considered unacceptable?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand you completely. You said DB operatives of the Krajina? Something like that? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me read you what you said. The question was from Mr. Farr: "Did you ever come across any information indicating that the State Security Department of the MUP of Serbia controlled any armed forces inside the RSK?" Your answer: "I don't have information to that effect. Although the frequent subject of discussions were various groups introducing themselves, and Martic at some point did say that these people should be talked to so that we could establish whether they were really members of the DB of the Republic of Serbia. He thought it unacceptable that they should be present in our area without us knowing about it." Was that Martic's view, individual view?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely as I put it. This was also an official position of the RSK government as well as Martic's, that nobody should be able to come to our area without having announced their arrival and let alone carry on any sort of actions. And that concerned everyone, be they our friends or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did Martic become, from 1991 onwards, increasingly paranoid about the presence of DB members in the Krajina working against him?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. And you've put it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we saw that, eventually, he was contacting Milosevic, accusing Kostic and Kojic, who he increasingly focussed upon, as DB members working against him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He did accuse them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now you spoke, on the 2nd of February - Your Honours, page 16892 onwards - about two government bodies or two government meetings, the Supreme Defence Council and the briefings. The briefings being the larger group containing around 50 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you told us that the Supreme Defence Council was, effectively, the paramount decision-making body in the RSK at the time?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Where it concerned the fields of defence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Basically anything to do with military operations was the business of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In practice?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would often happen that the Main Staff carried out an action and then informed the Supreme Defence Council about it subsequently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what he just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you repeat what you just said. The translator didn't pick it up, Mr. Draca.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the Supreme Defence Council was not a body which had as one of its powers to verify plans and actions of the Main Staff. The Supreme Defence Council would, in most cases, hear out the situation and the events in the fields of security and defence. At times, the Main Staff would come out with a plan and inform the Supreme Defence Council, but the Main Staff would proceed regardless of whether an approval was given by the council. In other words, the council could not give any sort of approvals or deny any sort of approvals to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who was in the Main Staff, please?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Army commander, Chief of Staff, and their deputies. I can name them, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Please do.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The period up to 1993, in autumn, there was General Mile Novakovic who was replaced by General Mile Celeketic up until the fall of the Krajina. Or, I'm sorry, no. He was removed after Operation Flash in Western Slavonia. And the last two months of the existence of the Krajina, there was General Mile Mrksic. He was the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the briefings, what kind of decisions were made at the briefings?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefings were attended by many lower-ranking commanding officers. Well, the command would report as well as the minister of the interior on the general security-related situation. Issues were raised about all the threats to security. At times, guide-lines and tasks would be issued to counter or improve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, you said, page 16898, in relation to a question by Mr. Farr, as to whether Ilija Kojic or Kostic attended the briefings, and you said: "No, they did not attend. I cannot remember if they ever attended any briefings like that, simply because it's a little bit too far for them to get organised and to come to that meeting. That was the only reason." So my question is: Kojic and Kostic were not part of the Supreme Defence Council, they were not part of the Main Staff, they didn't go to the briefings. What did they do in their sphere of influence or authority?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, Ilija Kojic was deputy minister of the interior for Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. Rade Kostic was assistant to the minister. There's a difference between the two positions. He was in charge of the area of Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But they appear not to have had any decision-making authority other the -- let's call it the Martic/Knin government or the Main Staff or the Supreme Defence Council. Was their sphere of influence, then, limited within a very limited region, the one that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you - this is my last subject, I hope - about -- could I -- about a particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: D398, please. Could we have that on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is a confidential document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you just have a look at this document and read through it just to see if you are able to assist with any of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please indicate when you want to go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can move on to the next page. Next page, please. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware at the time of this attempt by Arkan, Bozic and others to try to remove Kojic from his post?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was widely known in Krajina. This was in February of 1992. I don't think I worked there. Or I'm not sure that I was there. I didn't see the date. Which was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 19th of February, 1993, is the date of the document.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was working then.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know what Martic's position was? Do you know if he either intervened to protect Kojic or supported the attempt to remove him or remained neutral?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not remain neutral. He supported Kojic and wanted him to stay. But, as it says here, this was considered to be a conflict between Martic and Babic which was very intense at the time, so a reflection of that conflict was first felt in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, at some point, then, Martic's view changed and he wanted to get rid of Kojic. Do you know when that could be timed to, when that might have been, in relation to this incident?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time Martic was still minister of the interior. Only when he became the president of the republic did he embark on a conflict with Kojic and seek his replacement. But, as we know, this was later. Let's say a year after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D1588. There are redactions on this document. We have asked the -- perhaps it should be under -- private, please. We have asked the Serbian --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'd like to go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this document perhaps should not be shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before I move to this next document, Mr. Draca, was there anything in the paragraph that you read a moment ago in the previous document that you did not recognise as common viewpoints being expressed at the time, politically, within your service, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that is stated in that article is something that was known to me but also to the general public. For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is another state security report dated the 27th of February, 1995. And I'm interested -- and it's from the Novi Sad centre and I'm interested in the second paragraph where it notes: "Circles close to Martic are launching comments that one should not trust people 'connected' to Belgrade because their goal is to separate this area from the RSK. In order to disable these intentions, as it is stated, Martic is using military formation under Medic, Slobodan, aka Boco, and supporters of Miroljub Vujovic." Do you know anything about Martic responding to what he perceived to be a military threat from the likes of Kostic and Kojic by aligning himself with other military formations, such as the Skorpions and such as those revolving around Vujovic?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say here that Martic was constantly paranoid about conspiracies that Slavonia and Baranja would separate from the rest of the Krajina and join the Republic of Serbia, even though we tried to convince him often that this was not possible. But he would not give this up, and everything that would happen up in that area he would connect and ask to see if the Serbian DB had anything to do with that. This situation referred to in this paragraph is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know about Martic -- or did you hear about Martic visiting the Skorpions and seeking their assistance to -- as some form of security for him?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He tried to talk with him, but I don't know what the results of that were because all of us down there were against that, against including them in his personal security. But he did try.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And just to complete this, we've heard a lot about Kostic and Kojic and this -- their perhaps the Prosecution would term it a special unit or a military formation or whatever it was, did Martic ever complain that militarily they'd done anything other than operate a roadblock at Tovarnik, the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That was often the topic of what he said about that region and the conflicts with the local leadership there. That's something that he would talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So his complaint about Kostic and Kojic militarily was that they stopped him at the roadblock at Tovarnik. That was what their so-called unit was responsible for, according to Martic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Draca.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Petrovic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, may I tender the last two documents, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1588 will receive number D688, Your Honours. And document 1D5299 will receive number D689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Farr.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have an objection to both, pending receipt of information on provenance, and an objection to 1D1588, now marked as D688, pending the removal of the redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. Yes. Provenance for the first one, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May they be MFI'd, and we'll send the Prosecution the relevant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, one second, please. D688 and D689 are marked for identification. Mr. Petrovic, are you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both under seal. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Draca. Just a few more questions in order to clarify some of your answers over these past couple of days. You mentioned that you attended meetings of the Supreme Defence Council of the Krajina. You also mentioned the time when you attended those meetings. Are you able to tell us what sort of decisions were adopted, if any decisions were adopted, at these SDC meetings? What sort of decisions were they, if you're able to help us with this, please.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that some official decisions were adopted there, but mostly they were adopted by consensus, plans that had to do with security and defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who had the decision-making right at the SDC?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively President Martic. As the president of the republic, his was the last word, the final word.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you participated in these meetings as an associate member. You, as the deputy and chief of the department at that time, did you have the right to influence or amend decisions that were adopted at this body?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have that right. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned several times that Eastern Slavonia was specific in relation to the rest of the Krajina and that they were allowed to make some decisions independently. Are you able to explain why Eastern Slavonia was specific in relation to the rest of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was specific because it did not physically link up with the rest of the Krajina. I've already mentioned here that you needed to cross through two states and 6-, 700 kilometres in order to reach Slavonia and Baranja. Then, it was also specific by the fact that it was much richer by its economy, resources. Materially it was richer than the Krajina. And thirdly, it was specific because directly all of its boundaries touched on the Republic of Serbia, meaning that they lived normally. And in that way they traded, they bought things, they educated their children in a different way than the other part of the Krajina where we lived. And because of that, Martic constantly had this fear that they would secede from the Krajina and that is why he often was opposed to Slavonia and Eastern Baranja independently making decisions, and later, this was covered by legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what sort of decisions were adopted independently? From which sphere?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These decisions were adopted from all areas, except perhaps in matters of the Main Staff. The 11th Corps was directly involved in that, and the army much more respected these conventions than the civilian structures did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you were asked about the exchange of intelligence with the 2nd Administration, and in responding to these questions, you said that you exchanged information with other administrations as well. Are you able to tell us first which these other DB administrations in the Republic of Serbia did you exchange intelligence? If you know.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st and the 3rd Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what sort of information was exchanged with the 1st Administration?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mostly referred to counter-intelligence. We would inform that a person that we treated as a subject would be leaving and taking up residence in Serbia, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And why would this information be important to the 1st Administration of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, according to the classification then, that administration was dealing with that type of work: Counter-intelligence, security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned -- are you able to tell us, actually, how you would obtain information that would be of importance for the counter-intelligence service of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are measures and methods in the work of the DB, and I think it would be too long to explain that, but by work in the field, we would process persons of interest and then we would see whether a certain person was really working for some foreign intelligence service or not. And then if that person were to leave our territory and go to a different area, we would then inform the Republic of Serbia about that. During the war, such persons moved around a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you able to give us some examples? Do you know of any cases or subjects and some specific situations which would be of interest in the counter-intelligence area that you kept the 1st Administration informed about?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could give a lot of examples. I can recall many of them but I don't know -- these people are still working today in Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I don't know if I can mention examples in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would now like to move into private session so that the witness could give us this kind of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'd like us to look at P3076.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You reviewed the document yesterday with my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look at page 2. Page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And page 3 in English, please. Page 2 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the report makes mention of 118 different reports, dispatches, letters and Official Notes. Can you tell us what is the difference between the various categories of correspondence? What are dispatches? What are letters? And what are Official Notes?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A dispatch is an urgent report about an event, an individual, or similar. A letter, or a memorandum, is a letter whereby you are officially seeking something or giving an overview of the situation. An Official Note is an official document sent by a service to another in order to gain access to full information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, reference is made here to 118 different reports. In fact, they amount to two weekly reports on average?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At the time you headed the service, how many dispatches, letters, Official Notes and other forms of correspondence were produced on a weekly basis at that time?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm if this is realistic, this number of 118. But I can't see whether it says RDB here or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that you were asked to give your assessment on whether it was realistic or not. You were asked what the average number of weekly communications were when you were in charge. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may clarify, Your Honour. Maybe my question wasn't understood properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What I meant is, within your service, internally how many dispatches, notes or reports did you produce in a week?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean all together? Not just for the RDB of Serbia but all together?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the RDB of Serbia at all. I'm asking you now about your service and what the average weekly production of such documents was.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a huge number, over 200 letters a week. We had seven centres and four branches.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't catch plus what was the last bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You say 200 documents. What categories; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, documents as mentioned here. Dispatches, memos, Official Notes, plus monthly overviews, exchanges of information between the various centres, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. With Their Honours' leave, can you explain your puzzlement surrounding the 2nd Administration of the MUP? What was it that you wanted to clarify on this issue?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I noticed that there's -- this says the 2nd Administration of the MUP of Serbia. This sort of formulation doesn't hold. I'm afraid that this was an error and that these 118 various reports apply to all the administrations across the board. It doesn't say in this letter here, but we had a great many memos and dispatches to the public security. Far fewer to the RDB, although there were, and the correspondence of this sort has not been mentioned here at all. If you see, the next sentence says 28 reports of the RDB of the MUP of Republika Srpska, and that's properly recorded. I don't know if you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It has to do with the budget at the disposal of your service for the year 1993. It reads that the RDB had at its disposal 27.000 marks of which 15.000 were funds earmarked for the purchase of vehicles. It also reads that 9.000 German marks were allocated to the centres. What were the expenses covered in these centres, and how many employees did these centres have; if you know.

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the total of seven centres. Glina, Vojnic, Korenica, Knin, Okucani, Beli Manastir, and Vukovar, with branches at Benkovac, Srb Lapac and Darda. Funds, which were few, really, were provided to the centres for their overhead expenses, in fact, for, if you will, tyres for their vehicles to all sorts of other material, including office stationery, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do the 9.000 also involve travel expenses and other necessities?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It reads here that the remainder of 3.000 marks was used by the department. What is meant here? What were the expenses covered by the 3.000 marks in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department is headed by the chief. There's the deputy, the assistant heads of various administrations, and analysis. In other words, it's not a centre. And expenses were used in similar ways as they were in centres, for the same purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you view the capabilities of your service in the view of the funds that they had? Were they successful in performing their role?

utterances.speaker: ACO DRACA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically speaking, capabilities were next to none. But our work was based on operative work mainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, one element of your previous answer -- previous question was not answered. How many employees were covered by this budget?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I forgot to say that. Roughly 150 employees at that point in time, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Does that mean that the budget we are talking about doesn't cover any salaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The salaries were separate, directly from the Government of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. That's where we received our monthly salaries from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So budget is limited and -- that's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. * Q. Witness, do you know -- in 1993, to which year this report refers, do you know who was or who were the chiefs of the 2nd Administration of the Serbian RDB?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARR
utterances.text: This definitely doesn't arise from cross, and Mr. Petrovic had the opportunity to ask that on direct, if he were inclined to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend during his cross-examination suggested that all the reports were sent to the 2nd Administration.
